newsitem.title: JAPAN: Chief Japan nuclear investigator destroyed photos.
newsitem.headline: Chief Japan nuclear investigator destroyed photos.

text.p: The chief investigator of Japan's top nuclear agency deliberately destroyed photographs of the country's worst atomic accident last month, the state-run corporation announced on Wednesday.

In shock new disclosures about an incident which has turned into a major scandal, the Power Reactor and Nuclear Fuel Development Corp. (PNC) said cleaners had also first removed, and then replaced, debris caused by the accident.
A PNC statement revealed for the first time that eight cleaners had been exposed to low-level radiation in the cleanup after they misinterpreted orders to cordon off the area.
The statement said that, in view of the latest revelations, the team investigating the March 11 accident had been completely disbanded and replaced by a new group.
In the accident at Tokaimura processing plant, about 120 km (75 miles) north of Tokyo, there was a fire, and then an explosion caused by failure to extinguish the blaze properly.
The PNC announced at the time that a total of 37 workers had suffered low level radiation but did not mention the unnecessary exposure of eight cleaners.
The accident set off demands for a major review of safety standards in the nuclear industry, including calls for private companies to take over PNC operations.
The PNC was established in 1967 to carry out research, operate nuclear plants, recycle nuclear material and help Japan achieve energy self-sufficiency through nuclear power.
There were also calls for a review of energy-starved Japan's plans to expand its reliance on nuclear power from the present 33 per cent to 42 percent by 2010.
The demands grew on Tuesday after the shutdown of a nuclear power plant at Fukushima, about 200 km (125 miles) north of Tokyo, after a brief rise in radiation from exhaust gases.
The PNC's revelations about the role of its top investigator in taking a "sudden arbitrary decision" to destroy photographs added more fuel to the fire.

The statement said the investigator had decided to destroy the photographs, taken on the day of the accident, when he realised six days later he had not mentioned them in his preliminary report, even though their existence was known to plant workers.
The statement quoted the unnamed investigator as saying:
"I suddenly realised that, if we released the photos now, we would be thought of as having concealed them. I thought of making as if they didn't exist."
The destruction of the photographs recalled a similar incident in a 1995 sodium coolant leakage at Japan's prototype fast-breeder reactor, Monju.
In the Monju case, the PNC was first criticised for not releasing video film of the accident and then for editing the footage to show minimal damage.
The PNC said the eight cleaners at Tokaimura had been exposed to radiation when they misunderstood an order to cordon off the area for an instruction to clean up the area.
Without wearing protective clothing, they removed debris. When their mistake was discovered, they were ordered to replace the debris where they found it to help investigators.
Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto has apologised for an accident which investigations showed, even before Wednesday's revelations, to be a major bungle from start to finish.
Workers first mistakenly believed they had put out a fire in a bituminisation facility 12 hours before an explosion blew out windows in the building.
Plant officials falsified their report on the timing of the blaze, saying it was out before it even started.
They also violated requirements to inform residents and national authorities promptly of an escape of radiation.
